# FIELD_MAP: Validity, Conceptual Robustness and Confounding

> Field-map tensor of the area "VCRC". Methodology: .cursor/skills/build-field-map/FIELD_MAP_PLAYBOOK.md.
> The map carries only facts about the area (what a paper showed, which question it
> closes, where future-work points). No "where should WE dig" recommendations.
> English only. The `fieldmap-*` blocks below are the machine-readable source of
> truth parsed by scripts.field_map.parse_map into backend/content/maps/vcrc.json.

- **Axes (one line):** RQ (research question — the mandatory ROOT axis) × LOCUS (research/measurement-pipeline link) × THREAT (validity threat / mechanism) × VALIDITY (classic validity type) × DOMAIN (research subject / eval class) × INSTRUMENT (measurement instrument) — every axis read per paper from its own content, none privileged; recency + citation importance weighting active (as_of 2026-07). See fieldmap-giants for retained canon.
- **Catalog:** 3609 point-articles across 1702 distinct papers (grown axis-first from an initial curated seed corpus + a real arXiv discovery sweep exhausted to the tail; every paper carries a genuine cover-to-cover read; a full-catalog coordinate-verification pass then corrected 148 placements and dropped 2). 121 papers are citation giants (>100 Semantic-Scholar cites, as_of 2026-07).
- **future-work actually read:** 1702/1702 papers re-read >=2x and read cover-to-cover >=1x from cached full text (resweep read-ledger complete); citations refreshed for the full catalog (as_of 2026-07). Companion edges carry 1834 future-work edges under 19 canonical F-questions. `resweep check` PASSES on DEFAULT gates: catalog 1702 DISTINCT papers (need >=1000), re-read 2x 1702/1702, full-text 1702/1702, harvest 1702/1702, 3 trailing QUIET sweeps, schema OK.
- **Density (measured, not gated):** the rich 6-axis scheme is kept honestly (AXIS-FIRST — axes are never coarsened to inflate per-cell depth); density is MEASURED not gated by the corrected instrument, so no per-map override is used. Current: 1492 covered cells, 541 with >=2 studies (corroborated), 310 with >=3 (robust); a paper filling several cells counts toward each.
- **Companion:** FIELD_MAP_edges.md (future-work edges TSV; the paper -> question -> cell graph)

## Data blocks (machine-readable — parsed by scripts.field_map.parse_map)

```fieldmap-meta
id: vcrc
title: Validity, Conceptual Robustness and Confounding
tldr: Where and how the validity, conceptual robustness and confounding of empirical ML research break, mapped across the field's research questions.
as_of: 2026-07
```

```fieldmap-about
VCRC reads any empirical ML result as a measurement-and-inference chain and asks where its VALIDITY, conceptual robustness and confounders break. The ROOT axis RQ carries the field's research questions about validity (construct definition, construct/discriminant validity, operationalization fidelity, measurement reliability, sampling, contamination/gaming, evaluation awareness, annotation/ground truth, causal warrant, external/criterion validity, temporal validity, Goodhart, harness confounds, positive/negative validity evidence, reproducibility, fair comparison). The other axes are read per paper: LOCUS is the pipeline link the issue sits on; THREAT is the kind of validity threat or confound; VALIDITY is the classic validity type (construct / internal / external / statistical-conclusion / temporal); DOMAIN is the research subject / evaluation class; INSTRUMENT is the measurement instrument the finding rests on. A cell is one full coordinate point; the papers sitting there answer it, and authored empty points are research gaps. Papers are weighted by recency + citations so the current research front and the canon read heaviest.
```

<!-- RQ is the MANDATORY ROOT axis and MUST be the FIRST row of fieldmap-axes
(assembled in F0 from the seed brief + its links + papers' future-work, fold-or-create;
playbook §2 "RQ assembly"). Fill its `values` (RQ1…RQN) before parsing; parse_map
--check fails loudly if there is no RQ axis, if RQ is not first, or if any article
lacks an RQ value. Every later axis groups the articles to MEASURE coverage of the RQs. -->

```fieldmap-axes
RQ	Research question	["RQ1", "RQ2", "RQ3", "RQ4", "RQ5", "RQ6", "RQ7", "RQ8", "RQ9", "RQ10", "RQ11", "RQ12", "RQ13", "RQ14", "RQ15", "RQ16"]	The field's research questions about the validity, conceptual robustness and confounding of empirical ML research - the mandatory ROOT axis, assembled first from the seed brief and the papers' future-work. Each paper carries the validity question its finding answers, read from its own content.	{"RQ1": "Is the target construct defined and theory-grounded (nomological network, AI-native constructs) before a measure is built?", "RQ2": "Does the measure capture the intended construct and not a confounder or surface proxy (construct + discriminant validity)?", "RQ3": "Is the operationalization (items/tasks/prompts) a faithful, sufficiently-complex realization that does not leak format or shortcut cues?", "RQ4": "How reliable is the scorer/measurement instrument (LLM-judge variance and bias, item-response theory, statistical power, uncertainty)?", "RQ5": "Is the evaluation set representative and realistic, not convenience sampling, and does it cover the population?", "RQ6": "Can the evaluation be gamed, and can train/test contamination be detected (including under reinforcement-learning or evasive hiding)?", "RQ7": "Does the system behave differently because it knows it is being evaluated (evaluation awareness, sandbagging, reactivity)?", "RQ8": "Are per-item scores annotated and aggregated without annotator/label/ground-truth dependencies (annotation science, rater effects)?", "RQ9": "Is the causal inference about the system warranted, free of confounds, spurious correlations and shortcut features (internal validity)?", "RQ10": "Do results generalize to real-world / out-of-distribution outcomes (external / criterion / ecological validity, transportability)?", "RQ11": "How does validity drift over time and with scale (temporal validity, benchmark saturation, scaling-law validity)?", "RQ12": "How does optimization pressure corrupt the metric (Goodhart, reward hacking), and what principled limits exist?", "RQ13": "In agentic/protocol-heavy evaluations, how does the harness/scaffold/training setup confound what is being measured?", "RQ14": "How do we provide positive (confirmatory) and negative (red-team / falsification) evidence that an evaluation is valid?", "RQ15": "Is the empirical result reproducible and statistically sound (replication, significance testing, multiple comparisons, nondeterminism)?", "RQ16": "Are baselines and comparisons fair (tuning and compute parity, no leakage between conditions, sound ranking/aggregation)?"}
LOCUS	Pipeline locus	["Construct definition", "Operationalization", "Data sampling", "Measurement / scoring", "Score aggregation", "Statistical inference", "Generalization / deployment", "Experimental protocol / harness"]	Which link of the empirical-ML measurement-and-inference pipeline the validity issue sits on - read per paper from its own content.	{"Construct definition": "Defining the abstract target construct and mapping the real-world target onto it.", "Operationalization": "Turning the construct into concrete items, tasks or prompts.", "Data sampling": "Choosing which items/data make up the evaluation or training set.", "Measurement / scoring": "Scoring an output into a number (judge, metric, classifier, verifier).", "Score aggregation": "Combining per-item scores into a reported metric or ranking.", "Statistical inference": "Drawing statistical conclusions (significance, uncertainty, power) from the scores.", "Generalization / deployment": "From the measured score to the real-world / out-of-distribution deployment claim.", "Experimental protocol / harness": "The surrounding experimental setup, agent scaffold, tooling or training protocol that runs the study."}	{}
THREAT	Validity threat	["Construct misrepresentation", "Confounding", "Contamination / leakage", "Gaming / Goodhart", "Unreliability / variance", "Sampling bias", "Reactivity / evaluation awareness", "Reproducibility failure"]	The kind of validity threat or confound the paper concerns - read per paper from its own content.	{"Construct misrepresentation": "The measure under- or mis-represents the intended construct (a surface proxy).", "Confounding": "A confounder or spurious/shortcut feature breaks the causal link between score and construct.", "Contamination / leakage": "Train/test overlap, memorization or look-ahead leakage inflates the score.", "Gaming / Goodhart": "Optimization pressure or adversarial manipulation corrupts the metric.", "Unreliability / variance": "Noise, instability or scorer bias make the measurement unreliable.", "Sampling bias": "The evaluation set is unrepresentative or convenience-sampled.", "Reactivity / evaluation awareness": "The system behaves differently because it detects the evaluation.", "Reproducibility failure": "Results fail to replicate across runs, setups or implementations."}	{}
VALIDITY	Validity type	["construct", "internal", "external", "statistical-conclusion", "temporal"]	The classic validity type (Cook & Campbell taxonomy) the finding bears on - read per paper from its own content.	{"construct": "Whether the measure captures the intended theoretical construct.", "internal": "Whether the inferred causal relationship is free of confounds within the study.", "external": "Whether the result generalizes to other populations, settings and times.", "statistical-conclusion": "Whether the statistical inference (significance, power, uncertainty) is sound.", "temporal": "Whether validity holds over time and across scale (drift, saturation)."}	{}
DOMAIN	Research subject	["capability", "safety", "honesty", "fairness", "generation-quality", "code", "reasoning", "general-methodology"]	The research subject or evaluation class a paper's finding concerns - read per paper from its own content.	{"capability": "Capability or general benchmark-performance measurement (knowledge, psychometrics, leaderboards).", "safety": "Safety-oriented evaluation (jailbreaks, harmfulness, guardrails, misuse, alignment).", "honesty": "Honesty / truthfulness evaluation (hallucination, factuality, faithfulness, lying).", "fairness": "Fairness / bias / demographic-disparity measurement.", "generation-quality": "Open-ended response-quality / preference evaluation (NLG, summarization, translation, judges of quality).", "code": "Code-generation / software-engineering evaluation.", "reasoning": "Reasoning / math / logic evaluation.", "general-methodology": "General empirical-ML methodology not tied to one task (statistics, causal inference, reproducibility, measurement theory)."}	{}
INSTRUMENT	Measurement instrument	["LLM-judge", "statistical / metric", "human", "rule-based / verifier", "classifier / probe", "none / theoretical"]	The measurement instrument a paper's finding rests on - read per paper from its own content.	{"LLM-judge": "An LLM acts as the scorer/judge of the output.", "statistical / metric": "A statistical estimator or metric produces the score (IRT, conformal, error bars, correlation, power analysis, psychometrics).", "human": "Human annotation or rating is the scoring instrument.", "rule-based / verifier": "A deterministic rule, exact-match, unit test, programmatic verifier or contamination detector produces the score.", "classifier / probe": "A trained classifier or activation probe produces the score.", "none / theoretical": "No measurement instrument - a theoretical, position, taxonomy or survey work."}	{}
```

P273	Robustness to Distributional Assumptions of Benchmarks	https://arxiv.org/pdf/2404.16966	Melissa Ailem, Katerina Marazopoulou, Charlotte Siska, James Bono	2024	{"RQ": "RQ5", "LOCUS": "Data sampling", "THREAT": "Sampling bias", "VALIDITY": "external", "DOMAIN": "general-methodology", "INSTRUMENT": "statistical / metric"}	["benchmark-robustness", "sampling", "construct-validity"]	Demonstrates that the standard average-over-test-prompts protocol assumes representativeness, and that reweighting the benchmark's prompt distribution changes which model wins, exposing sampling assumptions as a threat to benchmark conclusions. P273	Robustness to Distributional Assumptions of Benchmarks	https://arxiv.org/pdf/2404.16966	Melissa Ailem, Katerina Marazopoulou, Charlotte Siska, James Bono	2024	{"RQ": "RQ15", "LOCUS": "Score aggregation", "THREAT": "Unreliability / variance", "VALIDITY": "statistical-conclusion", "DOMAIN": "general-methodology", "INSTRUMENT": "statistical / metric"}	["benchmark-robustness", "sampling", "construct-validity"]	Quantifies how the reported aggregate score varies under alternative distributional weightings of the same items, arguing benchmark accuracy needs sensitivity analysis rather than a single point estimate. {"DOMAIN": "capability", "INSTRUMENT": "LLM-judge", "LOCUS": "Construct definition", "RQ": "RQ1", "THREAT": "Construct misrepresentation", "VALIDITY": "construct"}	[{"name": "Independently corroborated (a second study reports it)", "covered": false, "by": []}, {"name": "Robustly established (three or more studies)", "covered": false, "by": []}, {"name": "The field's follow-up requests here are resolved", "covered": false, "by": []}]	To deepen this point: only one study sits here (not yet independently corroborated); the field still asks: Although we attribute these results in part to social desirability bias — that is, SMs avoiding hostile or morally conflictual content when they infer they are being assessed — we cannot directly distinguish this from a genuine representational limitation. The present design does not include a condition that suppresses or bypasses alignment-related avoidance, so the relative contribution of social desirability bias versus representational constraint remains an open question (F5); help verify that SCORS-G ratings reflect meaningful narrative differences rather than surface-level scoring artifacts (F4).
{"DOMAIN": "capability", "INSTRUMENT": "LLM-judge", "LOCUS": "Construct definition", "RQ": "RQ2", "THREAT": "Construct misrepresentation", "VALIDITY": "construct"}	[{"name": "Independently corroborated (a second study reports it)", "covered": true, "by": ["P617-2", "P840-1", "P893-1"]}, {"name": "Robustly established (three or more studies)", "covered": true, "by": ["P617-2", "P840-1", "P893-1"]}, {"name": "The field's follow-up requests here are resolved", "covered": false, "by": []}]	To deepen this point: the field still asks: Automated Evaluation Bias: Although MUSE demonstrates strong correlation with human judgment, MLLM-based auditing may overlook visual nuances or the affective experiences of users in subjective dimensions (F2); In-the-wild evaluations inevitably encounter dynamic elements (e.g., A/B testing, real-time ads, network latency). Such environmental noise poses a risk where failures caused by external interference are misattributed to agent incompetence (F7); This highlights that high scores often result from surface-level pattern matching rather than true scientific reasoning. SIQA provides the necessary tools to distinguish performative fluency from authentic competence, setting the stage for trustworthy AI in scientific practice, where both perceptual clarity and knowledge correctness are essential (F4).
{"DOMAIN": "capability", "INSTRUMENT": "LLM-judge", "LOCUS": "Data sampling", "RQ": "RQ4", "THREAT": "Unreliability / variance", "VALIDITY": "construct"}	[{"name": "Independently corroborated (a second study reports it)", "covered": false, "by": []}, {"name": "Robustly established (three or more studies)", "covered": false, "by": []}, {"name": "The field's follow-up requests here are resolved", "covered": false, "by": []}]	To deepen this point: only one study sits here (not yet independently corroborated); the field still asks: Paraphrases were GPT-4o generated with semantic filtering; formal human adjudication with inter-annotator agreement would strengthen validation (F9); We did not evaluate calibration side effects (Expected Calibration Error, false positive/negative shifts) (F3); low flip rate does not imply visual grounding: text-only baselines show that some models stay consistent even when the image is removed, suggesting they rely on language priors (F7).

If a question can be answered without visual input, perturbing the image is meaningless... This constraint highlights an important boundary: our method is only effective when visual semantics directly determines the correct answer (F17); Future progress will therefore require not only larger or more expressive models, but also stronger transferable structural priors, richer benchmark tasks, and tighter links between benchmark robustness and experimentally validated RNA function (F8); Future work should focus on improving the comparability and verifiability of reported results through automated leaderboards, standardized evaluation protocols that reduce metric heterogeneity, and more robust contamination detection methods (F18); Limitations Our benchmarking framework can ensure strictly contamination-free evaluation with a fully automated building workflow, but (F1); The high plausibility scores indicate that these hallucinations are sophisticated enough to deceive standard text-based evaluation metrics, posing a significant safety risk (F2); The sandbox isolates by relocation rather than containerization, which removes leakage through relative paths and environment but not a determined search for the evaluator by absolute path, so competitive use would want host-level containers (F14); With one case per family per split, a ranking over 41 points is statistically fragile, though the generator makes enlarging the sample inexpensive (F10); a reference solver and an evaluator built on the same kernels can share the same mistake and still agree, so their agreement confirms the contract but cannot, by itself, certify the evaluator’s underlying physics (F9); background scenes, soil appearance, and lighting conditions are partially shared across classes (F7); the automatically-generated nature of the Dots evaluation data inevitably carries biases compared to the data distribution of real-world TOD settings (F19).

{"DOMAIN": "fairness", "INSTRUMENT": "statistical / metric", "LOCUS": "Construct definition", "RQ": "RQ2", "THREAT": "Construct misrepresentation", "VALIDITY": "construct"}	[{"name": "Independently corroborated (a second study reports it)", "covered": true, "by": ["P1044-2", "P1518-1", "P678-2", "P698-1", "P796-2", "P853-1"]}, {"name": "Robustly established (three or more studies)", "covered": true, "by": ["P1044-2", "P1518-1", "P678-2", "P698-1", "P796-2", "P853-1"]}, {"name": "The field's follow-up requests here are resolved", "covered": false, "by": []}]	To deepen this point: the field still asks: Given the rapid release of LLMs, political alignment remains a moving target. Our results reflect models available in late 2025. Establishing a longitudinal auditing benchmark would allow researchers to track alignment shifts across model generations (e.g., from Llama 3 to Llama 4) (F12); In the future, we advocate that predictive representativity analysis (and analogous subgroup fairness evaluations) become a standard component of model validation and risk assessment (F19); Our behavioral audit relied on consensus labels from media monitors, which provide high-level categorizations of outlet bias. While effective for detecting broad systematic shifts, these labels do not capture article-level framing nuances or temporal variation in outlet stance. Future work could leverage expert-annotated corpora with paragraph-level ideological tagging to enable finer-grained analysis of how LLMs interpret lexical choice, framing, and entity selection (F9); Our psychometric analysis utilized instruments heavily rooted in Western political philosophy (e.g., the Political Compass and 8Values). While these frameworks are standard in political science, they may not fully capture the ideological nuances of non-Western contexts, such as collectivistic versus individualistic orientations in East Asian political thought or the secular–religious dynamics prevalent in parts of the Global South. Future research could adapt this methodology to culturally localized political inventories to determine whether the observed “Libertarian Left” drift is a universal artifact of English-language pre-training or a specifically Western alignment phenomenon (F15); Through this work, we are looking forward to developing a method to debias such systems and developing a metric to measure gender bias without treating it as an immutable binary concept (F4); Validating PictoPercept against behavioral outcomes in realistic decision contexts would strengthen claims about its predictive validity for real-world inequality (F8); While we carefully controlled for confounding variables including attractiveness and trustworthiness, other perceptual features not captured in CFD norming data may influence judgments (F7).

Minor lexical or syntactic changes (e.g., modality, presuppositions, evaluative wording) can shift label posteriors and thus bias measurements, creating a degree of freedom in how tendencies are quantified (F17); Bias-laden terms and political descriptors often carry language-specific connotations that may not transfer, potentially confounding cross-lingual comparisons. Thus, some language effects may reflect translation artifacts rather than model behavior (F15); Our analysis captures biases at a specific temporal snapshot and does not claim long-term stability (F12); Our metrics capture entity priors under controlled prompts. Depending on the task, differences may reflect associations, stereotypes, or world-knowledge-like priors rather than normative unfairness. This situation follows broader critiques that “bias” metrics reflect specific measurement choices and may conflate distinct constructs Blodgett et al. ( 2020 ) (F4); We focus exclusively on structured, classification-style tasks and do not evaluate open-ended text generation (F8).

reliance on human raters, which is expensive and time-consuming. In the future, we plan to develop more generic automatic evaluation methods that approximate human ratings, helping people develop better models (F4); A vote-aware selection system that increases the probability of selecting less-played models and lowers it for more-played ones is needed, and we plan to explore this in future Arena improvements (F18); A/B testing in a production environment would be needed to verify that the generated headlines actually improve click-through and search ranking (F8); As motion generation techniques continue to advance, the samples used in our study may not accurately represent error distributions in future improved models, potentially affecting the determination of the best metric (F12); BLEU scores collapse compared to English, casting doubt on the metric’s suitability for evaluating non-task-specific systems (F15); For documents exceeding approximately 27,000 words, the evaluation component itself may yield unreliable quality assessments, producing a cascading error scenario where erroneous evaluation feedback propagates to misguided refinement operations (F3); Future efforts could standardize evaluation protocols by defining a minimal set of shared metrics and listener test formats to ensure reproducibility (F11); Future metrics should especially take this last aspect into account, and improve their robustness to adversarial conditions (F17); Future work could explore automatic evaluation aligned with our taxonomy, improved annotator training, and the use of synthetic data to augment test collections and facilitate the development of ATS models that better mitigate these errors (F9); Negatively-weighted references could have a greater effect if, for example, randomly extracted responses had also been annotated (F19); Second, our work did not extensively address the bias in using GPT-4 for evaluation, which we consider an important topic for future research (F2); The next step is selected via greedy decoding, yielding a single solution trajectory and one SE score per model per question (F14); aesthetic predictors may encode latent content preferences shaped by the training data or annotator biases (F7); ## §0 Tensor axes and legend

The map is a 6-axis coverage tensor over the validity, conceptual robustness and confounders of empirical ML research. **RQ** (root) carries the field's 16 validity research questions; the other five axes are read per paper from its own content and are never privileged: **LOCUS** (which pipeline link the issue sits on), **THREAT** (the validity threat / confound), **VALIDITY** (the Cook & Campbell type), **DOMAIN** (research subject / eval class) and **INSTRUMENT** (the measurement instrument the finding rests on). A cell is one full coordinate point; the papers there answer it. Papers carry recency + Semantic-Scholar citation weighting (`as_of 2026-06`). Coverage tiers below are DERIVED from the per-cell aspect checklists, never authored.

## §2 Article catalog (tensor atoms)

All 270 catalogued papers, grouped by their root **RQ** value. Each atom: **Pxx Title** [link] · authors year · DOMAIN/THREAT/INSTRUMENT · tldr.

## §8 Main tensor findings (aggregation + golden threads)

The catalog concentrates on **judge/measurement reliability (RQ4, 66 papers)**, **contamination/gaming detection (RQ6, 50)**, **discriminant/construct validity (RQ2, 28)**, **confounds/shortcuts (RQ9, 26)**, **operationalization fidelity (RQ3, 17)** and **annotation/ground-truth (RQ8, 15)** — the operational, day-to-day validity threats — while the temporal/scaling-and-agentic-harness frontier (RQ11, 2; RQ13, 7), the positive+negative validity-evidence frontier (RQ14, 6) and the construct-definition upstream (RQ1, 5) stay deliberately thin.

**Thin-RQ audit (all 270 re-scanned vs RQ1/RQ5/RQ11/RQ14).** A full second pass judged every paper against the four thin root values to separate genuinely-sparse from under-detected. It re-homed five papers: four meta-evaluation contributions whose deliverable is validity evidence for an evaluation (ground-truth/controlled-intervention/simulation meta-eval) moved into **RQ14 (6)**, and the measurement-modeling theory paper moved into **RQ1 (5)**. The other two thin values are confirmed **sparse-by-corpus**: **RQ5 (sampling / representativeness, 4)** — genuine population-coverage / convenience-sampling work, as opposed to external-validity/transportability (12 in RQ10) — and **RQ11 (temporal / scaling validity, 2)** — drift-over-time / saturation studies, as opposed to scaling-aware measurement methods that live in RQ4 — are rare in this evaluation-validity literature, not merely undetected.

**Convergent future-work demand** (distinct source papers asking each canonical question):
- **F1** (46 papers): Make benchmark contamination/leakage detection reliable and evasion-resistant (incl. RL post-training, multimodal, multilingual).
- **F3** (31 papers): Quantify and calibrate judge/measurement uncertainty, noise and variance.
- **F8** (24 papers): Validate generalization to out-of-distribution, real-world and deployment populations.
- **F9** (23 papers): Improve annotation reliability, rater models and ground truth under disagreement.
- **F2** (20 papers): Remove systematic biases from LLM-as-a-judge (position, verbosity, self-preference, style, language).
- **F7** (18 papers): Remove shortcut/spurious reliance and confounds, ideally without group annotations.

**Golden threads** (across-paper warnings that recur):
- *A score is not its construct.* Contamination, judge bias and shortcut features all let a number rise while the latent property it claims to measure does not — construct validity must be argued, not assumed (RQ2/RQ6/RQ9).
- *The judge is an instrument with its own error.* LLM-as-judge and metric scorers carry position/verbosity/self-preference bias and run-to-run variance; uncalibrated, they manufacture false precision (RQ4, F2/F3).
- *Validity decays.* Benchmarks saturate and contaminate over time; a result valid at release is not valid at scale or later (RQ11, F12).
- *Statistical rigor is the exception, not the rule.* Significance, multiple-comparison control, power and error bars are routinely missing from ML evaluation (RQ15, F10).

## §8-bis Quality-deepening verdicts (re-harvest + fat-RQ + axis audit + gap validation + fat-DOMAIN + cross-axis combination)

**1) Weak sources repaired.** 21 catalogue papers whose cached full text was an ar5iv error page (`No content available` / `Untitled Document`) or abstract-only were re-fetched from the arXiv PDF (pymupdf) to real full text — 0 weak-source pages remain (every paper is now backed by genuine full text, harvest 270/270). Re-judging the repaired papers against the clean text corrected 4 coordinates: P053 (DOMAIN reasoning -> general-methodology); P081 (INSTRUMENT none / theoretical -> statistical / metric); P230 (RQ RQ4 -> RQ8); P268 (DOMAIN reasoning -> generation-quality); the other 17 held.

**2) Fat-RQ audit (RQ4, RQ6).** The two over-stuffed roots were re-scanned paper-by-paper (119 papers). 5 were re-homed out of **RQ6** where the word "contamination" meant training-noise robustness or adversarial judge-gaming rather than eval-data leakage (P071 RQ6->RQ15; P113 RQ6->RQ12; P121 RQ6->RQ4; P175 RQ6->RQ12; P247 RQ6->RQ4); the remaining 114 placements were confirmed. Post-move the busiest roots are **RQ4 (66)** and **RQ6 (50)**.

**3) Secondary-axis consistency audit.** LOCUS/THREAT/VALIDITY/DOMAIN/INSTRUMENT were each given a dedicated cross-paper pass (all 270 grouped by value, plus an oddity shortlist of rare RQ×value pairings). Verdict: **clean** — the rare pairings were small RQ clusters or genuinely rare-but-correct combinations, so no secondary-axis value was reassigned.

**4) Gap / frontier validation.** All 16 required-uncovered (red) cells and 22 greenfield questions were judged against their converging future-work demand (canonical Fk requests) and structural coverability (Hamming-1 covered neighbours, per-axis support): **38/38 real, 0 spurious** — frontier confirmed - every red cell and greenfield question is a real, field-demanded, coverable gap; 0 spurious; no correction/re-rebuild needed.

**5) Fat-DOMAIN audit (general-methodology).** The largest DOMAIN value, the catch-all **general-methodology** (98 papers), was re-scanned paper-by-paper to test whether it was a lazy dumping ground. It is not: the bucket is genuinely task-agnostic methodology — benchmark contamination detection/mitigation (RQ6), causal-inference / confounding / spurious-correlation methods (RQ9), conformal & robust statistics and reproducibility (RQ4/RQ15), leaderboard-aggregation methodology (RQ16), and measurement-theory / construct-validity FRAMEWORKS, REVIEWS and CRITIQUES (RQ1/RQ2/RQ3). 5 papers were re-homed to **capability** because their primary deliverable is a PSYCHOMETRIC MEASUREMENT administered to models (the P074/P101/P106/P243/P155 genre), not measurement theory (P085 -> capability; P168 -> capability; P210 -> capability; P233 -> capability; P262 -> capability); the other 93 held. New DOMAIN distribution: general-methodology (93), generation-quality (48), reasoning (36), capability (26), safety (26), honesty (15), code (14), fairness (12).

**6) Cross-axis combination audit (THREAT x VALIDITY + borderlines).** The secondary-axis consistency pass (3) only checked single (RQ x value) pairings; this pass scrutinised the PAIRS of secondary axes. All 270 papers were grouped by every pair of LOCUS/THREAT/VALIDITY/DOMAIN/INSTRUMENT, surfacing 9 THREAT x VALIDITY outliers (a validity rare within its threat's own distribution, cell <=2 papers) plus the near-singleton value pairs; every flagged paper was close-read (full text for the 9 outliers + the 3 borderlines P053/P247/P121). Verdict: **0 moves** — each rare pairing is a deliberate, correct tag (e.g. contamination-over-time as temporal validity, evaluator-uncertainty confound producing a spurious statistical effect, eval-awareness reactivity established by a causal intervention), so no coordinate was reassigned. The 22 greenfield questions were also checked for near-duplication: **0 duplicate** region targets or idea strings — each anchors a distinct red cell.

## §9 Deep-dive on the central RQ (RQ4 — scorer/measurement reliability)

RQ4 is the field's busiest validity question (66 papers): *how reliable is the scorer/measurement instrument?* It spans instruments — LLM-judge (42), statistical / metric (17), classifier / probe (5), none / theoretical (1), rule-based / verifier (1) — across domains — generation-quality (33), safety (9), general-methodology (7), reasoning (4), honesty (4), fairness (4), code (3), capability (2).

- **What is established.** LLM-as-judge bias (position, verbosity, self-preference, style) and high run-to-run variance are robustly and repeatedly demonstrated; the cell on judge unreliability is one of the few well-covered points.
- **What is contested.** Whether bias-correction and calibration (debiasing prompts, panels of judges, conformal/IRT uncertainty) actually recover the latent construct, or merely move the error around, is unresolved across papers.
- **What is missing.** Calibrated uncertainty that travels to deployment, judge reliability under optimization pressure (judge × Goodhart), and reliability of judges in safety/honesty domains where ground truth is itself unreliable — these are the red cells and the F3 convergence.
- **Cross-cutting link.** RQ4 feeds RQ8 (annotation/ground-truth) and RQ12 (Goodhart): an unreliable instrument cannot anchor a fair comparison (RQ16) or a generalization claim (RQ10).

## §10 Open questions (question summary from the edge graph)

The future-work graph holds **259 questions** (237 paper-sourced + 22 greenfield) folded into **19 canonical questions**. The heaviest unmet demand:

- **F1** — Make benchmark contamination/leakage detection reliable and evasion-resistant (incl. RL post-training, multimodal, multilingual). *(asked by 46 papers)*
- **F3** — Quantify and calibrate judge/measurement uncertainty, noise and variance. *(asked by 31 papers)*
- **F8** — Validate generalization to out-of-distribution, real-world and deployment populations. *(asked by 24 papers)*
- **F9** — Improve annotation reliability, rater models and ground truth under disagreement. *(asked by 23 papers)*
- **F2** — Remove systematic biases from LLM-as-a-judge (position, verbosity, self-preference, style, language). *(asked by 20 papers)*
- **F7** — Remove shortcut/spurious reliance and confounds, ideally without group annotations. *(asked by 18 papers)*
- **F4** — Establish construct validity (nomological nets, measurement modeling, psychometrics) for AI evaluations. *(asked by 10 papers)*
- **F11** — Make ML evaluation reproducible across runs, seeds, setups and implementations. *(asked by 10 papers)*

The 16 red cells (§3-bis) are the empty points this demand converges on but no catalogued paper yet occupies — the field's concrete open frontier. Greenfield questions (22) mark asks the instrument itself raises (red-gap-anchored and cross-paper synthesis) that no single paper voiced.
